item.title: Power cuts and sleep: Students link load shedding to anxiety, disrupted rest and lower grades
item.description: South Africa endured its worst year of load shedding (scheduled power cuts by the country's utility, Eskom) in 2023. The power went off on 335 of the year's 365 days, often several times a day. Since then, the country has gone more than a year and a half without these planned power cuts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Glowing plants reveal immune responses around infection sites via two colors
item.description: Researchers at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS) have developed a new way to make glowing biological reporters more accurate, allowing scientists to track gene activity in living plants over days, weeks and potentially even months and years. The approach could help researchers study how plants respond to disease, pests and environmental stress, while opening the door to similar applications in animal and human disease models. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Before astronauts return to the lunar surface, NASA will first conduct one of the most ambitious and complex test missions in the agency’s history. Launching in 2027, Artemis III will send NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano aboard the Orion spacecraft into low Earth orbit […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: NASA’s Swift Mission Ends, Leaves Behind Scientific Bonanza
item.description: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has ended its science mission now that the spacecraft is orbiting less than 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth’s surface. The greater atmospheric drag at this height prevents the satellite’s telescopes from steadily gazing at their astronomical targets. Swift conducted its final observation on Oct. 20. It is expected to […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Counting magnetic flux quanta offers new way to measure photon numbers
item.description: Researchers at AIST have directly observed magnetic flux quanta generated in a superconductor by photon absorption and demonstrated a new principle of photon detection that identifies the number of photons based on the number of these flux quanta. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Giro histórico en Turquía: “Creo firmemente que la Formación Durupınar representa los restos enterrados del Arca de Noé”
item.description: Un equipo internacional de investigadores halló estructuras artificiales; los análisis mediante radares sugieren la existencia de restos de una embarcación milenaria Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: Christina Koch, antes de recibir el premio Princesa de Asturias: “Siento nostalgia de la Luna, pero nunca habrá ningún sitio mejor para vivir que la Tierra”
item.description: La astronauta de Artemis II reflexionó sobre la exploración espacial; destacó la importancia de cuidar nuestro planeta y explicó por qué considera necesario avanzar hacia Marte Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: 'It's pretty toxic… but just a little, I want to be like that': What young men think of manosphere content
item.description: Masculinity content promises young men self-optimization and success, but often delivers health harms, risk-taking, unattainable standards, gender stereotypes and misogyny. The latter is the strongest predictor of violent extremism. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists demonstrate AI-designed enzyme for drug synthesis
item.description: The new RFD4-Proteina unified generative model for protein design—created by the Institute for Protein Design (IPD) in collaboration with NVIDIA—uses advanced AI to generate entirely new protein sequences and structures, achieving computational design success rates five to 10 times higher than previous models and generating candidates five to 10 times faster. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chemically modified sugars enable direct nanostructure formation
item.description: Researchers at AIST have demonstrated the synthesis of nanoporous carbonaceous materials and carbonaceous materials with layered nanostructures through a simple process involving the chemical modification of common sugars such as sucrose and fructose. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The psychology of why we overpay for used cars—study points to left-digit bias
item.description: Consumers routinely ignore information when making purchases. They overlook the tax attached to a price, skim past ingredient lists and often fail to process exact numbers with any precision. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Designing better adsorbents to remove PFAS from water
item.description: A review by Tohoku University researchers identifies key molecular features that could guide the development of more effective materials for removing PFAS from water. The study is published in the journal ACS Materials Au. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Plain silicon grating reveals a hidden 'twist' in light from electron beams
item.description: In 1953, two physicists showed that an electron beam skimming past a grating emits light whose color depends only on the electron's speed and the grating's spacing. Known as Smith-Purcell radiation, this phenomenon has become a useful tool for building compact, tunable light sources and tracking particle beams without touching them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bacteria reinvent their weapons through selection, chance and gene swapping
item.description: Many of the most potent antibiotics originate from bacteria. A large proportion belong to a class of compounds known as nonribosomal peptides (NRP). They are produced by large bacterial enzyme machineries—the nonribosomal peptide synthetases, or NRPS for short. These function like molecular assembly lines: Similar to the stations in a car factory, where new parts are added to the car at each step, several specialized modules string together amino acid by amino acid to build a peptide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New marker panel and free web tool help track stem cells as they develop
item.description: How can the identity of pluripotent stem cells be determined more reliably during their differentiation? Researchers from the IUF—Leibniz Research Institute for Environmental Medicine and Heinrich Heine University Duesseldorf have systematically validated marker genes for this purpose and developed a web-based application for the automated classification of early cell fates. The study has been published in Stem Cell Reports. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can we stop antibiotic resistance from ruining promising drugs before they reach patients?
item.description: What if we could predict early in drug development which antibiotics bacteria are most likely to become resistant to? In a review published in Nature Reviews Microbiology, researchers from the HUN-REN Biological Research Centre, Szeged (HUN-REN BRC Szeged) and the Hungarian Centre of Excellence for Molecular Medicine (HCEMM) in Szeged propose a five-step decision-making framework that could help identify resistance risks early, refine promising drug candidates and prevent costly failures. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Potatoes could be the secret to better plant-based meat, say food scientists
item.description: Potatoes could hold the key to making better gluten-free plant-based meat, according to a new study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Everyday Mylar turned into a promising insulator for lunar habitats
item.description: Establishing a long-term presence on the moon will require solving challenges that are easy to overlook on Earth. Lunar temperatures, for instance, can vary from hundreds of degrees below zero to boiling, making effective insulation essential for lunar habitats. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chaos makes sense of market movements in a crisis
item.description: Research shows that crises do more than cause financial market volatility and falling share prices—they lead to markets becoming far more interconnected. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stellar collision may explain why Orion Nebula's planet-forming disks appear younger than its stars
item.description: The Orion Nebula is a large star-forming region visible to the naked eye. Some of the young stars in the nebula are surrounded by disks of gas and dust in which planets form. Radiation from the massive central star, 1 Ori C1 (Theta-1 Orionis C1), gradually strips material from these disks, giving them shapes that resemble tadpoles. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: RS-25 Engine Tests at NASA Stennis
item.description: Teams at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Oct. 21, 2026. The hot fire test lasted for almost eight-and-a-half minutes (500 seconds), the same amount of time RS-25 engines fire during launch of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, with a 111% power level. For each […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists uncover the molecular pillars that shape our cells' powerpacks
item.description: Mitochondria are the tiny powerpacks that supply most of the energy our cells need. Their ability to generate this energy relies on a distinctive architecture: two membranes, one tucked inside the other, separated by a narrow gap called the intermembrane space (IMS). This tiny space helps sustain the chemistry of energy production, making its organization critical to how these cellular powerpacks function. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mechanism behind PARP1-mediated DNA repair characterized, offering insight into targeted cancer therapy
item.description: When DNA is damaged, cellular processes respond and repair the DNA. Inhibiting DNA damage repair can be therapeutically beneficial in cancers with genetic vulnerabilities related to DNA damage response. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital have uncovered a mechanism behind how this process works, which may have implications for cancer treatment. The results were published today in Molecular Cell. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rare fossils reveal what ancient Denisovans may have looked like
item.description: Whenever anything is written about the Denisovans, the word "mysterious" is almost guaranteed to appear. That is because we just don't know a lot about this extinct human group that may have lived in East Asia from at least 300,000 to 45,000 years ago and was closely related to the Neanderthals. The main reason for that is a sparse fossil record. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Black holes spinning near maximum rate could split in two, calculations suggest
item.description: Two black holes can collide and merge into one. But could the opposite happen: could a single black hole split into two smaller ones? That question is explored in a new theoretical study: "When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies," published in the journal Physical Review D. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hoarders without borders: Study suggests investors aid international expansion
item.description: Venture capital firms can help young businesses expand internationally by providing funding as well as market knowledge, expertise and access to professional networks, according to a research literature review published in the International Journal of Management and Enterprise Development. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From sea anemone to human fertility: A new research organism for understanding meiosis
item.description: Every egg cell and sperm cell depends on meiosis, a tightly choreographed process in which chromosomes find their partners, exchange genetic material and then divide. When meiosis goes awry in humans, the consequences can include infertility, miscarriage and birth defects. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: An ancient virus in chimpanzee DNA switches off a gene that is active in humans
item.description: Humans and chimpanzees share almost all their genes. Despite this, our brains have developed in different ways. Researchers at Lund University in Sweden have now shown that a viral pandemic dating back several million years is likely to be part of the explanation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Paleolithic human DNA reveals east-west connections across Ice Age Europe
item.description: More than 30,000 years ago, people associated with one of Europe's major Paleolithic cultures (the Gravettian) were more interconnected than previously thought. An international research team led by the University of Vienna has uncovered new genetic evidence of long-distance connections between these populations. Published in Science Advances, the study combines genomic data from rare human remains with human DNA preserved in cave sediments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find key to predicting some El Niño events 12 months ahead
item.description: Scientists have identified the conditions that make it possible to predict some El Niño and La Niña events up to a year in advance, potentially giving communities and decision-makers significantly more time to prepare for weather extremes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA, Virginia Launch Power Partnership for Energy Security
item.description: NASA is helping to foster long-term energy security in Virginia. NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia, is partnering with the Virginia Department of Energy to support informed decisions for effective energy generation, delivery and use by providing solar, meteorological, and future weather risk datasets for energy system modeling and planning purposes. Under a new […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Charles G. Hatfield

item.title: AI is solving math problems that stumped humans. What comes next?
item.description: A few short years ago, asking AI to add two four-digit numbers together for a third-grade math assignment would have been a bad idea. Over half the time, the answer would be wrong, studies have shown. Long division or a "leaky tank" problem, an algebra class staple? Forget about it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Massive carbon stocks in grasslands are ignored by climate finance
item.description: Open ecosystems—nonforested landscapes such as grasslands, shrublands and savannas—can store vast amounts of carbon while supporting water supply, biodiversity and other ecosystem services. Yet the potential of open ecosystems to serve as natural climate solutions remains ignored by policies that privilege forests. So reports a team of researchers in a policy brief published today in PLANTS, PEOPLE, PLANET. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Disaster recovery work temporarily boosted short-term physical and mental benefits for men
item.description: New Northwestern University research aims to shed light on what drives inequalities among men in the aftermath of megadisasters. In such situations, men are often depicted as heroic leaders, and this study finds that many of them experience improved mental and physical health while assisting with recovery efforts. However, for some men, the boost is short-lived once recovery activities are completed, leading to emotional lows and potentially increasing the risk of suicide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Marine heat waves suppress nutrient use, reproductive flexibility in humpback whales
item.description: A new study led by University of Hawai'i (UH) at Mānoa researchers reveals how extreme ocean warming disrupts whale metabolism, nutrition and reproductive success and what the developing 2026–2027 El Niño could mean next. As climate change drives increasingly intense marine heat waves, scientists are uncovering how these extreme warming events disrupt the biology of humpback whales. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fear‑based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear
item.description: On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers watched a little girl counting petals on a flower. Her voice gave way to a man counting down, and then a nuclear blast filled the screen. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Strategic new protections could link 13 Pacific deep-sea reserves into connected network
item.description: Protected areas have been set up to shield deep-sea life from the impacts of seabed mining in the Pacific Ocean. However, new research led by scientists at Plymouth Marine Laboratory (PML) and published in Nature Ecology & Evolution highlights an opportunity to make these protections even more effective. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ALMA spots 'dragon egg' that may represent the earliest stages of massive star formation
item.description: Astronomers identified an exceptionally tiny core that may represent an early stage in the formation of a massive star. Located in an infrared-dark area called Dragon Cloud, the core is nicknamed the "dragon egg." The paper, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics, was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 5. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Gold nanoparticles unexpectedly alter process that controls electrical conductivity in organic devices
item.description: Researchers at Umea university thought gold particles would make electronic components emit more light. Instead, they discovered an unexpected effect that could be important for the future of organic electronics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Archimedes screw inspires single-molecule motor powered by electric current
item.description: Molecular machines are regarded as the next step in miniaturization. Their models can be found in living cells, where molecular motors convert energy and generate movement. Scientists have been working for decades to artificially replicate such systems. The 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded for this research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Open-source workflow makes spatial proteomics easier to use
item.description: Fabian Coscia and his team have published in Nature Methods an open-source workflow that makes Deep Visual Proteomics easier to use, adapt and scale. OpenDVP enables scientists to spatially map thousands of proteins inside cells and their cellular environments, while preserving their tissue context. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How autumn changes animal sexual behavior—including that of humans
item.description: In the Northern Hemisphere, days are getting shorter and temperatures are dropping—autumn has arrived. A common sign that winter is coming is trees losing their leaves. But did you know that autumn also sparks changes in animals' sexual behavior—including ours? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Elusive uranium 'sandwich' molecule isolated after more than 50 years
item.description: In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from The University of Manchester and Lancaster University have isolated and characterized uranocenium, the positively charged form of a landmark uranium compound called uranocene. The work shows that this long-sought molecule is stable, and that it behaves in a way that challenges how chemists usually think about bonding in heavy elements. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Taiwan warns of 'destructive winds' as Typhoon Champi batters island
item.description: A powerful typhoon pounded Taiwan on Friday as authorities warned of "destructive winds" and urged locals to shelter from the storm. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More than just the thrill: What are 'sensation seekers' looking for?
item.description: Why are some people more drawn to new and exciting experiences than others? This phenomenon is usually explained by the fact that so-called "sensation seekers" experience stimuli less intensely than other people and therefore need intense experiences to feel alive. However, the uncertainty of the experiences also plays a role, such as the thrill of not knowing what will happen. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Artemis I: Crystals of experimental detectors record radiation doses near the moon
item.description: Do cosmic radiation doses near the moon differ significantly from those received by astronauts in low Earth orbit? Experimental lithium fluoride detectors, installed aboard the Orion spacecraft during the Artemis I mission, have now made it possible to obtain preliminary estimates. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: DNA programs a cell-free material to build its own motors and move
item.description: Researchers have created a material that manufactures the proteins responsible for cell movement, without needing intact living cells. By embedding cell-free gene expression into a thin sheet of protein filaments, they were able to make the material wrinkle, rise into blister-like shapes and break into bundles that flow around one another. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mapping the cell: International research team investigates the endoplasmic reticulum
item.description: Human cells contain billions of molecules. To prevent complete chaos, these molecules and the reactions between them are organized within structures known as organelles. One of the cell's most important organelles is the endoplasmic reticulum, a dynamic network that extends throughout the cell and plays an essential role in cell growth. Using a method they developed themselves, an international team of molecular biologists and bioinformaticians has tackled the challenge of determining precisely which molecules make up the membrane of this organelle. The researchers have published their… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Pedal to the metal: NASA's Psyche heads toward asteroid belt
item.description: With a successful Mars gravity assist in its rearview mirror, NASA's Psyche spacecraft has fired up its thrusters and is accelerating toward the metal-rich asteroid of the same name. During the first leg of its journey, following an October 2023 launch, the mission used its electric propulsion system intermittently to maneuver into the right position to harness Mars' gravity for a propellant-saving speed boost and a slight trajectory change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rocket debris hitting US homeland is ‘embarrassing’ for China, says astronomer
item.description: A scorched hunk of metal that turned up in a US farmer’s cornfield may have handed China an awkward moment and technically an “international incident”, according to a British astronomer who has tracked rocket launches for more than 30 years. The farmer found the bowl-shaped object, measuring about 3.35 metres (11 feet) across, while harvesting corn in west-central Minnesota on October 14. Online, some residents joked that aliens had landed, while Chinese internet users said it looked like a... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: US drinking water could contain double the reported PFAS levels, model estimates
item.description: Common ways of reporting perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)—the man-made, so-called forever chemicals that pose environmental and health threats—could underestimate the concentration of PFAS in U.S. drinking water by as much as half, according to a study being published Oct. 23 in Cell Reports Sustainability. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA's Hubble charts path for Roman with gravitational lenses
item.description: A sweeping barred spiral galaxy marks the spot in this image, but the real treasure is the gravitational lens in the lower-right corner, where a distant background galaxy is being magnified and distorted by the gravity of a closer galaxy. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When computer science meets the alpaca immune system
item.description: After earning bachelor's and Ph.D. degrees in bioengineering with a focus on molecular biology, Will White, a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Computer Science at Tufts, was pretty certain his future research would involve things like DNA and proteins. What he didn't know was that alpacas would also be part of the equation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Christina Koch, astronauta del Artemis II: “La gente se preocupa por si cambiaremos la Luna igual que hemos cambiado la Tierra; esa es nuestra elección”
item.description: Tras completar con éxito el histórico sobrevuelo lunar, se conoció una frase que la astronauta de la NASA pronunció mientras realizaba la misión Artemis II Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: What makes glass good at conducting heat? Sound holds the key
item.description: Glass can keep a drink safely contained, protect a smartphone screen, or serve as a foundation for electronic components. But when it comes to controlling heat, this familiar material still holds some scientific mysteries. Now, researchers have identified a key factor governing how efficiently heat travels through silicate glass, offering a new guideline for designing glass materials for next-generation electronic devices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How to speak whale: AI uses eight to ten click sequences to predict sperm whales' feeding dives
item.description: Arriving on the Caribbean island of Dominica for the first time "feels a little bit like stepping into Jurassic Park," said Giovanni Petri, a professor in the Network Science Institute at Northeastern University London. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From 'gentle' and 'graceful' to the 'cane toad of the sky': How Australia turned on the common myna
item.description: The common myna is sometimes referred to as "Australia's most hated bird." Originally from South and Central Asia, the introduced species from the starling family is abundant, raucous and bold. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A quick squeeze helps CRISPR turn skin cells into neurons more efficiently
item.description: Human cells hold about two meters (6.6 feet) of DNA, folded and compacted to fit inside a nucleus. That packing is essential for life, but it creates a problem for scientists. Some of the genes that control a cell's identity are buried so deep in tightly packed DNA that gene-targeting tools such as CRISPR activation, or CRISPRa, struggle to reach them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Youth protests across Europe: The overlapping crises facing Gen Z
item.description: Young people are facing a future that feels increasingly uncertain. Although every generation experiences turbulence while navigating adolescence, the pressures experienced by Gen Z—those born between 1997 and 2012—are different and seem more pervasive. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Excavation reveals history of Portuguese village shelled after sheltering Spanish refugees
item.description: Led by Dr. Rui Gomes Coelho, assistant professor of historical archaeology, the research reveals ordinary people's attitudes toward hospitality and solidarity in 20th-century Europe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Time to tap into agriculture's hidden genetic potential
item.description: Modern agriculture's selective breeding of crops for particular requirements may now be a roadblock to further gains, prompting a trio of senior University of Queensland plant scientists to call for a new way forward. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Experiment shows when quantum 'cat' states stop bouncing back
item.description: Quantum systems can occupy superpositions, quantum states that combine different possibilities. For instance, a microwave field can be prepared in a superposition of an empty state and a state that contains microwave light. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hallan basura espacial dos veces en pocos días en medio de un "creciente riesgo de víctimas"
item.description: El lunes se encontraron restos en Indonesia, apenas unos días después de que un agricultor de Minnesota, al otro lado del mundo, informara del hallazgo de un enorme objeto metálico, que se cree que es basura espacial, en un maizal. Fuente: Clarín - Mundo.

item.title: Study finds lower rates of overweight among vegan-fed cats
item.description: A large-scale survey has found cats fed vegan diets had lower rates of obesity and related health problems than those fed conventional meat-based diets. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Singapore's longevity industry: The quest for eternal youth
item.description: In Singapore, the quest for eternal youth is no longer just a billionaire's fantasy. It's becoming big business. High-tech clinics, longevity labs and specialist companies all promise the same thing: slowing down the ageing process. From continuous metabolic monitoring and genetic testing to supplements and oxygen therapy, every aspect of the body is measured and optimised. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: Théo Collet

item.title: Hide-and-seek for treats offers a new window into cognitive decline in dogs
item.description: It is tough to watch a dog deal with issues associated with aging. A senior dog that gets lost at home or starts showing more anxiety may be exhibiting signs of dementia. But by the time these signs show up, the decline may have been underway for years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: One of Earth’s most powerful supervolcanoes is refilling with fresh magma
item.description: Deep beneath Japan’s Kikai caldera, a massive magma reservoir is refilling 7,300 years after one of the most powerful volcanic eruptions in Earth's recent geological history. Scientists used underwater seismic surveys to reveal a vast store of magma that appears to have accumulated since the ancient catastrophe. The discovery could help explain how supervolcanoes like Yellowstone and Toba rebuild their magma supplies. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Study highlights gender gap in AI media coverage in Spain
item.description: A media "glass ceiling" exists in news stories on artificial intelligence (AI) published in Spanish media in recent years: men are the main subjects in 41% of news reports, compared to just 5% featuring women. This is one of the findings of the report "InfoIA: Analysis of Information on Artificial Intelligence Published in Digital Media," conducted by the University Institute of Gender Studies at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (UC3M). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI agents can form political camps—and changing their conversation partners does little to soften their views
item.description: Give AI agents political positions, ask them to defend their views and persuade one another, and let them decide which contacts to keep. This recent experiment, published in Nature Communications, found that over repeated exchanges, something familiar emerged: opposing camps that increasingly prefer their own company. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dental implants can hijack your immune system, scientists discover
item.description: Researchers have uncovered a surprising reason dental implant infections often resist antibiotics: the implants themselves can contribute to the problem. Bacteria corrode titanium implants, releasing microscopic particles that hijack immune cells, trigger destructive inflammation, and accelerate jawbone loss. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: What is red crown rot? Expert explains emerging soybean pathogen
item.description: Red crown rot, a fungal disease of soybean, is not new to the Midwest. First reported in Illinois in 2018, the disease is now surging across the state and the region. Boris Camiletti, a plant pathologist at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, is leading the effort to understand and combat the scourge, along with the Crop Protection Network, the Illinois Soybean Association, the United Soybean Board and researchers in surrounding states. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Good to see you after all this time. Chinese scientists put a face to the Denisovans
item.description: Chinese scientists have finally put a face to the Denisovans, a mysterious species of ancient humans who were previously known only through the evidence of their DNA and fossil fragments. The hominids were thought to have lived in parts of Siberia and East and Southeast Asia thousands of years ago. The work of reconstructing their face was based on fossils excavated from Xujiayao, a major archaeological site in northern China’s Nihewan Basin, between 1976 and 1979. Scientists also confirmed that... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Holly Chik

item.title: Breakthrough PTSD treatment achieves 68% remission rate in clinical trial
item.description: A newly FDA-cleared PTSD treatment uses personalized brain mapping and magnetic stimulation to target abnormal brain activity, with a clinical trial reporting a 52% reduction in symptoms and 68% remission. Researchers believe the technology could transform PTSD care and pave the way for more precise treatments for other mental health conditions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Rocket Report: SpaceX says no thanks to military launches; Spanish rocket nearly ready
item.description: "We believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms." Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
item.description: MIT engineers have built a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that respond to flashes of light, allowing it to swim and steer through water. The breakthrough could pave the way for tiny, self-healing biological robots capable of exploring fragile environments that ordinary machines cannot safely navigate. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A tiny defect in a crystal reveals a big quantum surprise
item.description: Researchers have solved a long-standing challenge in understanding how tiny defects in materials like diamond and silicon carbide behave when exposed to light. Their new computational method revealed a surprisingly important energy-loss mechanism in silicon carbide that scientists had previously underestimated. The finding helps explain a mystery that has puzzled researchers for years and could improve the design of quantum computers and sensors. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s
item.description: A seven-year study found that people with Parkinson’s disease who were more physically active experienced slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities. Those exercising more than eight hours per week showed almost no average cognitive decline, suggesting that staying active may offer important benefits as the disease progresses. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Paper straws worse for the environment than plastic, South Korea study finds
item.description: Paper straws, widely promoted as an eco-friendly alternative to plastic, may actually have a greater environmental impact than conventional plastic straws, according to a South Korean government-commissioned study that has renewed debate over whether switching materials truly reduces waste. The Comprehensive Study on Single-Use Straws, commissioned by South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment, was disclosed on Wednesday by opposition People Power Party lawmaker Kim Wi-sang, The... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: SCMP’s Asia desk

item.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
item.description: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Canadian conservation club with just 4 members to donate nearly 100-acre forest to university for honeybee research
item.description: A conservation club plans to transfer nearly 100 acres of land on Thorah Island to the University of Guelph. This site has been dedicated to honeybee breeding research for over thirty years. The donation aims to maintain the land for conservation and research instead of development. The University of Guelph will continue its long-term apiary operation critical to honeybee genetics work. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Just 3% of the world's glaciers account for over half of glacier ice loss
item.description: Glaciers ending in lakes, oceans or ice shelves make up 3.2% of the world's glaciers, but lost 134 billion metric tons (148 billion tons) of ice each year between 2000 and 2019, accounting for more than half of all glacier ice loss, a new study shows. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain
item.description: A tiny region deep within the brain has surprised scientists by revealing a remarkably sophisticated communication system. Previously thought to broadcast the same chemical signal throughout the brain, this region actually sends targeted messages that help control learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research in mice. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Light-based method enables precise control of ultrafast electron flow in a scanning tunneling microscope
item.description: What would it take to watch an electron move through a material? Researchers would need to see individual atoms and capture an electron's motion at incredibly short timescales. A Technion-led team has brought those two capabilities together in a scanning tunneling microscope, using carefully shaped laser pulses to control the direction of electron flow while preserving nanoscale spatial resolution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Costly dead-tissue disorder in apples caused by faster growth rates
item.description: New research reveals that faster growth rates in Honeycrisp apples increase both the incidence and severity of the "bitter pit" disorder, which is responsible for large-scale fruit yield losses and avoidable economic impacts for apple producers and storers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Iris patterns offer a noninvasive way to recognize individual Amazonian treefrogs
item.description: Identifying individual animals in the wild has long meant tagging, branding or clipping. For amphibians, the standard approach has often been toe-clipping, a procedure that can affect survival, physiology and behavior. A new study suggests that, for at least one species of treefrog, nature has already provided a more humane solution: the eyes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth from Space: The pink city
item.description: Image: This image shows a detailed view of the city of Toulouse in southwest France, with its terracotta tiled rooftops lending it the nickname la ville rose, or the pink city. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.description: That's our jam 🎼 Astronomers used our Chandra X-ray Observatory to find out that this radio wave formation, known as the "Treble Clef" thanks to its... Fuente: NASA.

item.description: Menopause is a natural stage of life, yet there's still so much misinformation surrounding it. Women deserve accurate information, proper care, and to have their concerns taken seriously. Naam Maın Kıa Haı Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: A mineral from the inside of planets reveals a surprising lesson: How you push matters
item.description: In the deepest region of the Earth's mantle, just above the core, much of the material consists of crystals of magnesium oxide. In larger rocky exoplanets called super-Earths, the higher pressures in the lower mantle may drive magnesium oxide to transform into a new high-pressure crystal structure or a metallic, electrically conductive liquid that generates a magnetic field. And in gas giants, magnesium oxide could exist in the cores themselves. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI was used to uncover a security weakness that affects most of the world's websites, researchers said. Here's what internet users should know.
item.description: AI was used to uncover a security weakness that affects most of the world's websites, researchers said. Here's what internet users should know. CBSNEWS.COM What to know about the PHP bug affecting 70% of the world's websites Fuente: CBS News.

item.title: Googly-eyed buoys and kites help keep seabirds out of fishing nets, study finds
item.description: Off the coast of Cornwall in southwest England, a pole rises from a buoy with a pair of big eyes on top. The head spins, creating what researchers call an “animated eye effect.” Its job is to scare away seabirds away before they dive into the fishing net below. On other nets, a kite shaped […] Fuente: Mongabay.

item.title: Mother bats' hearts beat faster at the sound of their own babies' cries
item.description: A mother bat has one crucial challenge: find her own babies among hundreds of other bats in the colony. Making sure she cares for and nurses only her own offspring is important to ensuring their survival. Among Japanese house bats, mothers keep track of their pups using the babies' isolation calls. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: El Niño Then and Now
item.description: A 35-year satellite altimetry record lets scientists hold this year’s El Niño up against its strongest predecessors. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: 40 years later, Chernobyl's nuclear fallout is not what scientists expected
item.description: Forty years after the Chornobyl disaster, tiny radioactive particles still linger in the soil, carrying a dangerous legacy. Using powerful X-rays, scientists discovered that some of these particles have remained surprisingly stable, trapping radioactive substances inside instead of releasing them into the environment. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How we mark our ballot can affect how we feel about voting. Here's why
item.description: Have you ever left a polling place feeling that your mark on the ballot didn't quite say what you wanted it to? Perhaps you liked two candidates but had to drop one, or backed the one who might actually win over the one you preferred. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nearly 3,000 exploding stars challenge our understanding of the Universe
item.description: A massive analysis of 2,884 exploding stars has uncovered new evidence that dark energy, the mysterious force accelerating the universe’s expansion, may change over time. The findings challenge a cornerstone of modern cosmology and could reshape our understanding of how the universe works. Fuente: ScienceDaily.
